sections.title: What you know
sections.content: You know *quien* from B1 Unit 5 and *el que* / *la que* after a preposition from B1 Unit 20 (*la persona con la que hablé*). You also know that the verb after *que* takes the subjunctive when the thing is only wished for or does not exist. Nothing changes when a preposition comes first: the mood still depends on whether the thing is real.

sections.title: The preposition goes first
sections.content: English likes to put the preposition at the end: "a person I can talk to". Spanish never does. The preposition comes before the relative word: *una persona con la que pueda hablar*. For people you can use *quien* (plural *quienes*); for people or things you can use *el que*, *la que*, *los que*, *las que*.

sections.title: Preposition + relative + subjunctive
rows: Necesito a alguien con quien pueda hablar.
I need someone I can talk to.
Busco una persona en la que pueda confiar.
I'm looking for a person I can trust.
Queremos un lugar en el que podamos descansar.
We want a place where we can rest.
No hay nadie a quien pueda preguntar.
There is nobody I can ask.

items.spanish: Tengo una amiga con la que puedo hablar de todo.
items.english: I have a friend I can talk to about everything (a real friend).

items.spanish: Necesito una amiga con la que pueda hablar de todo.
items.english: I need a friend I can talk to about everything (I don't have one yet).

items.spanish: Buscamos un lugar donde podamos trabajar.
items.english: We are looking for a place where we can work.

items.spanish: No hay nadie en quien confíe tanto como en ti.
items.english: There is nobody I trust as much as you.

sections.content: The preposition belongs to the verb inside the relative clause: *hablar con*, *confiar en*, *preguntar a*. Ask which preposition that verb needs, and put it before *quien* or *el que*. For places, *donde* often replaces *en el que*: *un lugar donde podamos descansar*.
